Anomaly detection for quality control

Visual inspection without defect images

Most AI inspection tools need many images of every defect before they work. VisionInspect needs only good parts: it learns what good looks like and flags anything that differs, including defects nobody has seen before.

Request a demo contact@visioninspect.de
  • Trained on good parts only
  • Flags unknown defects
  • One pass/fail limit
  • Runs offline

The problem with defect images

On a good line, defects are rare, and a new product has none at all. Collecting and labelling enough examples of every defect type can take months, and the next defect may look different from all of them.

Anomaly detection turns the problem around. Instead of learning what bad looks like, it learns what good looks like, and everything else stands out.

How it works

  1. 01

    Show it good parts

    Take a reference photo, mark the area to inspect and add photos of good parts.

  2. 02

    Automatic alignment

    Every photo is aligned to the reference picture, so parts don’t have to sit in exactly the same place.

  3. 03

    Heat map and score

    For each new part, areas that differ from the good parts light up in a heat map, and the part gets a score.

  4. 04

    One limit, PASS or FAIL

    You set a single pass/fail limit. The score turns into a clear verdict for every part.

Three ways to automate visual inspection

Rule-based machine visionDeep learning with defect classesAnomaly detection (VisionInspect)
What you provideRules programmed for each featureMany labelled images of every defectImages of good parts
New or unknown defectsOnly if a rule happens to cover themOften missed, as they were never trainedFlagged as a deviation from good
Setup effortMachine vision expertiseCollecting and labelling defect dataGood samples and one limit
Best forExact measurements, codes, fixed featuresSorting defects into known classesFinding any deviation from a good part

Where it works well, and where it doesn’t

Works well

  • Parts that look the same every time

  • Defects that are rare, varied or new

  • New products with no defect history

  • Electronics and PCBs, metal, plastic, glass and painted surfaces, packaging

Less suited

  • Exact measurements against tolerances: that is a job for gauging

  • Parts whose good appearance varies a lot: this needs more good samples, and zones to leave out areas that change

  • Naming the defect type: it shows where a part differs, not what the defect is called. The optional AI second opinion can add a written comment.

Surface defects on any material

Because it compares with good parts instead of looking for one defect type, the same approach finds scratches, dents, contamination, print errors and missing or extra parts on metal, plastic, glass or painted parts, as well as missing items in packs and boxes.

Questions

How many good samples do I need?

It depends on how much your good parts vary. For the bent-pin example on this page, one good board was enough. Start with a set of good parts, then use the Test step. If OK parts are flagged, add them as good samples.

What about harmless variation between good parts?

Good parts that are flagged can be added as good samples, or marked “this was actually OK”, and the model takes them into account. Zones let you leave out areas that change from part to part.

Can I add defect images anyway?

Yes. You can add bad samples to check that your pass/fail limit is right, but you don’t have to.

Do I need a data scientist?

No. It’s built for the people who run the line. There are no model names or settings to tune, only one pass/fail limit.

Does any data leave my network?

Not by default. Everything runs locally and works offline. Only if you turn on the optional AI check are images of failed parts sent, to the AI account you configured.
